sources.title: 'Houston, We've Had a Problem': 50 Years Ago, Apollo 13 Crisis Timeline
sources.supported_claim: Timeline of the explosion (55:54:53 GET), initial ambiguity between an instrumentation glitch and a real event, confirmation of oxygen tank 2 reading zero, Kranz's near-immediate order to prepare a Moon-loop return using the LM descent engine, and the fact that using the LM to maneuver the stack had already been studied as an SPS-failure contingency.

sources.title: Apollo 13 Flight Journal / Apollo 13 mission transcripts (Day 3: 'Free Return' and 'Lifeboat')
sources.author_or_institution: NASA / Apollo Flight Journal (W. David Woods et al., hosted by NASA History Office)
sources.date: Mission conducted April 1970; journal compiled and annotated later from mission transcripts
sources.supported_claim: Ground-elapsed-time details of the free-return trajectory correction burn (61:29:42 GET, ~31 seconds) and the later PC+2 burn (079:27:40 GET, ~14.8 seconds), based on mission transcripts and flight logs.

sources.title: Lost Moon: The Perilous Voyage of Apollo 13
sources.citation: Lovell, J., & Kluger, J. (1994). Lost Moon: The Perilous Voyage of Apollo 13. Houghton Mifflin. (Republished as Apollo 13.)
sources.supported_claim: Commander Lovell's first-person account of the explosion, the crew's role in the trajectory decision, and the reasoning for treating the Lunar Module as a 'lifeboat' rather than risking the Service Module main engine.

sources.title: 13 Things That Saved Apollo 13, Part 4: Using the LM for Propulsion
sources.date: Retrospective article, drawing on 1970 mission records and NASA engineering accounts
sources.supported_claim: Detail that the Service Propulsion System engine was mounted immediately adjacent to the damaged oxygen tank bay and that its condition after the explosion was unknown, and Gene Kranz's own description of a strong reluctance ('foreboding') to fire that engine.

sources.title: How the Crew of the Damaged Apollo 13 Came Home
sources.supported_claim: Consumables constraint: the Lunar Module was designed to support two men for roughly two days on the lunar surface but was pressed into supporting three men for about four days; water was the most acute shortage, requiring severe rationing.

sources.title: Apollo 13 crisis: carbon dioxide scrubber canister incompatibility and the improvised adapter
sources.author_or_institution: NASA History Office / NASA Mission Details page
sources.supported_claim: That the Command Module's square lithium hydroxide CO2-scrubber canisters did not fit the Lunar Module's round receptacles, that this became a dangerous CO2 buildup roughly a day and a half after the crew moved into the LM, and that the improvised 'mailbox' fix was devised by ground engineers after the trajectory decision had already been made and acted on.

sources.title: Report of Apollo 13 Review Board
sources.author_or_institution: NASA Apollo 13 Review Board (chaired by Edgar M. Cortright)
sources.citation: NASA Apollo 13 Review Board. (1970). Report of Apollo 13 Review Board. Washington, D.C.: NASA.
sources.supported_claim: Official post-flight finding on the root cause of the explosion (damaged wiring insulation in oxygen tank 2, linked to a ground-handling incident and an incompatible heater/thermostat design), used to support what was not knowable to the crew or Mission Control during the mission itself.

sources.title: Apollo 13
sources.supported_claim: General chronology cross-check: mission dates, splashdown on April 17, 1970, and the mission's outcome and legacy.
